# Answers: AI Leadership

English · [Русский](../ru/answers/leadership.md) · ← [AI Interview Atlas](../../README.md)

Written answers to the priority questions of this track, in the same order and numbering as *Start here*. Answer each question yourself first: what follows is one good answer, not the only correct one, and an interviewer is listening to your reasoning rather than checking your wording.

Answers written: 40 of 40.

### 1. An assistant reads external email, searches internal documents and sends replies. Where could an attacker redirect it, and how would you constrain the damage?

*System design · [Safety, security and governance](../themes/safety-security-governance.md)*

Incoming mail lands in the same context as instructions, while the assistant's authority is wider than the sender's rights: a message asks it to find an internal document and forward it outside, and the model obliges. You do not fix that with prompt wording, you fix it by separating levels. Untrusted mail content stays data, and the authority to search or send lives in a tool layer that never reads a message as a command. I would narrow the tool set, restrict recipients to the current thread and known addresses, and require explicit human approval to go beyond that or to attach files. I would test against a corpus of indirect injections and exfiltration attempts, measuring the share of outbound messages carrying data above the requester's access level. The risk does not disappear: injection filters miss things, and data can still leak through an allowed channel.

Read: [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)

### 2. How would you organise safe deployment of an AI model into production?

*System design · [Safety, security and governance](../themes/safety-security-governance.md)*

A release starts with intended use: its task, affected users and unacceptable outcomes. Then risk becomes a shared artifact rather than a team opinion. Threats are written down, an assessment is done, and every role has a name on it: who evaluates, who accepts the residual risk, who is on call during an incident. The cost is obvious, the release goes slower and some of the work does not look like development. In practice I would expose the system in stages, from internal users to a share of traffic, hold thresholds on an eval set together with production signals like complaints, harmful responses, latency and cost, and rehearse rollback in advance with a clear trigger and a named owner who can stop it. The limit is simple: a procedure cannot anticipate every risk, so the assessment is repeated when the model, the data or the load changes.

Read: [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) · [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

### 3. How would you approach safety for a generative-AI consumer product?

*Product case · [Safety, security and governance](../themes/safety-security-governance.md)*

Safety for a consumer product is designed from a concrete use case and audience, not from a general list of prohibitions: who these people are, why they come, what abuse looks like here, and what harm is real for vulnerable groups. Then it is not one barrier but several layers: product limits on what the service simply does not do, model evaluation on an abuse corpus, a live reporting channel, and escalation to a human where the cost of error is high. Every layer costs money and friction, so measure both sides: the share of harmful completions and the share of unnecessary refusals, always broken out by user segment, language and topic. I would run a regular review of reports and feed them into the eval set. The limit is that the set always lags behind new abuse patterns, and averaged metrics hide harm concentrated in a small group.

Read: [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) · [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)

### 4. What safeguards should surround an AI system that acts on a user's behalf?

*System design · [Safety, security and governance](../themes/safety-security-governance.md)*

The key distinction is that the model proposes an action and the system authorises it, and those are different subsystems. Authority is scoped to the user, the resource and the operation: the agent acts no wider than the rights of the person it acts for, and a token is issued for a specific operation rather than for the whole account. Consequential and irreversible actions are shown to a human in plain wording: what exactly, to whom, for how much. Policy is checked at execution time on the service side, because a check inside the prompt can be talked around. You need an action log with an end to end identifier, spending and rate limits, and a recovery plan for partial completion, where a compensating operation matters more than a blind retry. The boundary is confirmation fatigue: ask about everything and people stop reading, so confirm what is expensive and irreversible.

Read: [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/) · [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

### 5. Describe a situation where delivery pressure conflicted with security or safety concerns. How did you decide what to do?

*Behavioral · [Safety, security and governance](../themes/safety-security-governance.md)*

Answer this as a risk decision, not as a story about saving the day. Take a real episode and start with the hazard: what specifically could have happened, who it would have affected, and what evidence you had at the time, including what you did not know. Then name the alternatives you considered seriously, such as narrowing the launch, enabling it for a subset of users, adding manual review, or moving the date, and say who had the authority to accept the remaining risk and how you escalated. That is what the interviewer is listening for: whether you separate your own opinion from someone else's decision, and whether you know who owns the risk. The common failure is the hero who saved everyone, or a decision with no author. Finish with an honest result, including what went wrong, and the control that changed afterward.

Read: [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

### 6. How would you improve ChatGPT for enterprise customers?

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

Improving an enterprise assistant starts with a segment and one workflow, not a feature list. I would look for a recurring task where the answer already exists inside the company but is expensive to find and assemble, for example drafting a response against internal policies, and describe a specific user and the point where they get stuck. Then an honest comparison: if search, a template or rules solve it, the model is not needed. For enterprise customers demos do not decide anything, integration and trust do: sign in through corporate accounts, permissions inherited from the source, logging, and requirements on data storage and processing. I would bound the pilot with an outcome announced in advance: time on task, share of tasks finished without rework, quality guardrails, and the condition for expanding. The weakness of pilots is that enthusiasts do not predict behaviour under mandatory rollout.

Read: [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/) · [Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)

### 7. A model offers much greater capability but costs ten times as much. How would you decide what product to build with it?

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

The question is whether gains make previously untrusted tasks acceptable: where mandatory human review was required before and spot checks are now enough. You count not the price of a token but the cost of a successfully completed workflow, including retries, review and the cost of error, because an expensive model that passes on the first attempt is often cheaper than a cheap one with three attempts and a review. You pay in latency, complexity and dependence on a single provider. I'd measure that cost on my own task set, test willingness to pay on a narrow segment, and turn on selective routing: the expensive model only for hard cases or cases where an error is costly, the cheap one as the base. The limit is that if users don't notice the difference in outcome, no quality gain pays for itself, and prices and capabilities move faster than product plans.

Read: [Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml) · [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/)

### 8. How do you decide whether an LLM is useful for a proposed product problem?

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

I start from the user's job and the baseline solution, not from the model: their goal, how it is done today, and what a mistake costs. If rules, search or a simple model close the task, that is the answer, a simple heuristic and a clear metric first, otherwise you add complexity with no gain. Then I check four things: whether we can access the data, whether the result can be evaluated at all, whether the scenario tolerates latency, and whether variability in the answer is acceptable. Where reproducibility and exact calculation are required, the model is at best an interface over a deterministic system. Then a bounded comparison on a shared task set with thresholds and cost stated in advance. I always name the reason to reject the approach up front, or the pilot succeeds whatever happens. This tells you about suitability, not about whether the feature gets used.

Read: [Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml) · [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

### 9. Design a Gemini-based assistant for university students.

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

I would drop the universal helper and pick one segment with one recurring need, say first year students preparing for an exam in a specific subject, and make the course materials the source rather than the whole internet. The flow is built around understanding: the assistant works through the mistake, asks questions back and points to the place in the materials instead of producing the finished assignment; uncertainty is stated out loud, and copying is treated as the main abuse model and limited in the product, with academic integrity rules in mind. I would measure task success, learning value through a delayed knowledge check, and only then retention. That is exactly where the boundary runs: retention can grow from harm, because students love an assistant that does the work for them even though it makes their learning worse, and without a learning metric you will not see it.

Read: [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/) · [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

### 10. Users say Gemini gives incorrect answers with excessive confidence. What would you change?

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

First I would stop treating this as one problem and split the complaints by cause: the model does not know the fact, retrieval brought back the wrong thing or nothing, or the answer is presented so that the confidence does not match the grounds. Those are three different fixes. Grounding in sources reduces invention but adds latency and moves quality onto retrieval; abstention can reduce exposure to wrong answers but irritates people when it fires without reason; interface changes like showing citations and marking unverified claims are cheap and shift trust without touching the model. So I would compare those options on the same task set rather than by feel, and watch the share of claims with no source support, useful task completion, and regressions by segment. Calibration aligns confidence with observed correctness; it does not fix factual errors. Abstention and interface choices change exposure, and warnings may be ignored.

Read: [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) · [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

### 11. How would you prioritise features for an AI writing assistant in Microsoft Word?

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

Prioritisation starts by splitting writing into distinct tasks: drafting from scratch, rewriting an existing passage, shortening, fixing tone and grammar, and merging several documents. For each I'd find the point where the person gets stuck today and compare expected value, quality risk, engineering cost and dependencies such as access rights to the document. The risk here is asymmetric: a suggestion next to the text is cheap when it is wrong, while a sweeping edit of someone else's document is expensive, so tasks with a visible, reversible result on a selected fragment come first. The first release should be narrow, and I'd measure not the volume generated but the assistance a user accepted: the share of inserted text still in the document later, and the share of undos. The limit is that acceptance is not quality, people accept an edit to avoid arguing, so text quality needs a separate check.

Read: [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/) · [Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)

### 12. How would you measure success for an AI feature in a Microsoft product?

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

The metric starts with the user's goal and an observable sign the task is done: what exactly should happen in the product if the feature worked. Then I would separate the layers people usually mix: adoption, meaning who tried it, retention, who came back, task quality, whether it was finished and how many edits or undos there were, plus latency and cost per task. Model metrics on the eval set stay, but as an explanation of cause, not as proof of value. You pay for this in event instrumentation and discipline about definitions. You compare against a baseline or inside an experiment: how the task was done without the feature. And think in advance about how the metric will be gamed, through pushy suggestions or counting an impression as usage. A short experiment will not see trust effects that take months to appear.

Read: [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/)

### 13. What North Star metric would you choose for an AI search product, and what would constrain it?

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

I would make the headline metric the share of sessions with a usefully completed search task, not clicks and not time on page, because both rise when the answer is bad. Completion has to be observed indirectly: the user did not rephrase, went through to a source and did not come straight back, took the next action; some cases need human labelling because the behaviour is ambiguous. Any single metric pushes you to an extreme, so you add guardrails around it: the share of claims with no source support, safety, latency and cost per query, and a regression in any of them cancels the gain. I would explain the denominator separately: do we count sessions or queries, what we do with bots and repeats, how we segment by language and task type. For navigational and entertainment queries completion is poorly defined, and there the metric misleads.

Read: [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/)

### 14. Notification engagement rises while total time spent remains flat. How would you interpret that result?

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

The most likely explanation is substitution: notifications do not create activity, they move it out of organic visits, so total time does not change. But before explaining behaviour I would check the measurement: do the definitions of engagement and time match, did impressions simply grow, are cohorts of new and existing users mixed together, and was this an experiment with a control or a before and after comparison. Then the substantive question: do notifications lead to actions that would not have happened otherwise, or to the same actions just earlier. Look at opt outs and unsubscribes, complaints, satisfaction and retention over a long horizon, because a short term rise in clicks is often paid for by losing the channel. Finally, flat time does not by itself mean there is no value: the product may have become more useful in less time, and that is a fine outcome.

Read: [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/)

### 15. Choose an AI agent or product you use and propose its most valuable improvement.

*Product case · [AI product strategy and metrics](../themes/ai-product-strategy.md)*

Answer this through an observed breakage rather than a wish list. Take a product you use regularly and describe the moment it fails you: an agent loses context between sessions and makes you explain the task again, or it confidently goes off in the wrong direction with no way to intervene while it runs. Then explain why the improvement you chose outranks the alternatives, how often the situation happens, what it costs the user, whether a workaround exists, and in doing that you show prioritisation rather than taste. Then name the cheapest way to test the hypothesis, a success criterion stated in advance, and a likely adverse effect: keeping context raises privacy risk, and allowing interruption slows the work down. The boundary is that you are reasoning as a user from outside, so do not invent another team's internal reasons, plans or metrics.

Read: [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/)

### 16. Define a strategy for an internal AI platform, including who owns its success metrics.

*Product case · [AI platform and operating model](../themes/ai-operating-model.md)*

An internal platform strategy starts from noticing that several teams are doing the same work: getting access to models, assembling evaluation, setting up logging, dealing with secrets and personal data. The platform takes what repeats and leaves teams what is unique to them, otherwise it becomes a bottleneck. I would split the metrics by level: the platform owns reliability and demand, meaning gateway availability and SLO, time from idea to working prototype, the share of teams that chose it voluntarily, and cost per request; the business outcome stays with the consuming teams, because otherwise nobody owns it. In practice, pick one workflow and support it end to end, say explicitly what the platform does not do, and set a date in advance to review continued investment. If internal teams have no right to choose an alternative, the adoption number stops proving anything.

Read: [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/) · [Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications](https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/)

### 17. How would you support multiple model providers when some deployment environments permit only a subset of models?

*System design · [AI platform and operating model](../themes/ai-operating-model.md)*

The environment's allowed list must govern model selection. The route is computed from data class, jurisdiction and the policy of the specific environment: the application asks for a capability such as long context or image input, and the platform picks a permitted model and can explain why that one. A portable interface over providers hides the shape of the call, but it must not hide the differences: context length, tool support, structured output format and guardrail behaviour diverge, and believing models are interchangeable turns into regressions in production. So capabilities are declared explicitly and checked with a shared eval set on every allowed route. Fallback is permitted only inside the allowed set, and when no compliant route exists the request is rejected with a clear error instead of quietly going to another provider. The price is less flexibility and constant upkeep of the environment matrix.

Read: [Architect multitenant solutions on Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/overview) · [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

### 18. Tell me how you handled an engineer who was not meeting expectations.

*Behavioral · [Leading engineering teams](../themes/engineering-leadership.md)*

The interviewer isn't listening for a firing story; they want to see how you separate facts from impressions. So build the answer from the observable gap: what expectations were written down, which results and deadlines missed them, and which examples show it. Then explain how you gave feedback: directly, promptly, not in public, and what you heard back. The causes usually sit in unclear priorities, skill gaps, or circumstances outside work. Name the support you offered, the actions you agreed with a check-in date, and how it ended, including the cases where the person left. One common mistake is opening with a diagnosis of their personality and closing with a moral; another is staying silent about your own part in expectations never being clear. Finish with what you changed in your own practice: how you state expectations now, and how early you notice drift.

Read: [[re:Work] Google's New Manager Training Slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/13-rj7ZqlyuHNli9Ybd5D8g-qqUNtG81t3JLq7JV5c2o/htmlpresent)

### 19. How did you handle a high-performing engineer whose behaviour caused conflict with colleagues?

*Behavioral · [Leading engineering teams](../themes/engineering-leadership.md)*

Separate two things in your first sentence: the person's technical contribution and the consequences of specific behaviour. Otherwise the answer sounds like a complaint about someone's character. Describe what was observable: whose work got held up, who stopped bringing ideas, which meetings ended without a decision. What's being tested is whether you set standards for collaboration as clearly as you set them for results, and whether you quietly make an exception for a strong engineer. Say how you talked one on one, what you heard back, since sharpness often covers overload, unclear authority, or a sense that quality is being sacrificed, and what behaviour changes you agreed in checkable terms. End with what you saw afterwards and what would have followed if nothing changed. The mistake is finishing with "we talked and it went away"; the interviewer wants the follow-up, not a happy ending.

Read: [[re:Work] Google's New Manager Training Slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/13-rj7ZqlyuHNli9Ybd5D8g-qqUNtG81t3JLq7JV5c2o/htmlpresent)

### 20. Describe how someone you mentored progressed in their career.

*Behavioral · [Leading engineering teams](../themes/engineering-leadership.md)*

Start with their goal, not your role: what they wanted to reach, where they stood then, and what gap to the next level was visible in their work. Then explain what the mentoring actually did: which tasks you helped them pick or handed over, what questions you asked, what feedback you gave and how often. What is being listened for is whether you grow people through real work and whether you avoid taking credit for their wins, so name the achievements as theirs: they did it, they defended the design, they got promoted. State your own contribution separately and more modestly: you created an opportunity, removed an obstacle, made the result visible. The common mistake is a story where the mentor decides everything and the mentee only executes. Finish with what you learned about developing people and what you do differently with the people you lead now.

Read: [[re:Work] Google's New Manager Training Slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/13-rj7ZqlyuHNli9Ybd5D8g-qqUNtG81t3JLq7JV5c2o/htmlpresent)

### 21. What do you do when your team disagrees with your proposed direction?

*Applied scenario · [Leading engineering teams](../themes/engineering-leadership.md)*

First I work out what the disagreement is about: facts, a forecast, or priorities. Otherwise the discussion goes in circles. I ask people to name the assumptions my proposal rests on, then take the strongest objection and state it better than its author did: if it falls apart, the direction is firmer; if it doesn't, I'm the one who has to change the decision. Where the argument turns on an unknown quantity, it's cheaper to run a bounded experiment or prototype with an agreed criterion than to keep arguing; the price is time, so I fix the deadline up front. Then I say plainly whose call it is: the discussion is open, the responsibility is mine. The decision, reasons and rejected options go into a design doc with the conditions for revisiting it. This is overkill when a decision is cheap and reversible: then trying is faster than aligning.

Read: [Design Docs at Google](https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/)

### 22. How would you respond when a high performer considers leaving during a reorganisation?

*Applied scenario · [Leading engineering teams](../themes/engineering-leadership.md)*

I start with a conversation that isn't a negotiation: I want the reason, not retention at any price. Then I separate the temporary uncertainty of a reorganisation, an unclear manager, an unsettled team shape, plans on hold, from problems that predate it: a growth ceiling, pay, relationships, the content of the work. The mechanism is simple: the first is treated with information and dates, the second only with real changes. Confusing them is expensive, because a promise I can't keep speeds the exit and costs the team's trust. So I say honestly what is decided, what I influence, what is still open and when it will be known. I offer support I can actually give, write down unresolved questions and set a follow-up on a specific date. If the reason is beyond my influence, the goal changes: a decent exit, a handover and a preserved relationship are a result too.

Read: [Organizational Change Management](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/people-group/organizational-change-management/)

### 23. How would you stabilise an engineering team after a change in management?

*Applied scenario · [Leading engineering teams](../themes/engineering-leadership.md)*

I spend the first weeks listening rather than reforming: one on ones with the team and with key partners, asking what gets in the way today and what people are afraid of tomorrow. A change of manager by itself lowers predictability, so any big early change reads as a threat, even a sensible one. Then I put clarity back: which priorities hold right now, who owns which decisions, which meetings and reports stay and which go away. Urgent risks to delivery and to people I close immediately, without waiting for the full picture. After that I make a small number of changes, each with a stated reason, and check the effect after a fixed period against dates, incidents, attrition and direct feedback. This pace is wrong if the team is already in crisis: there you stop the fall first and listen as you go.

Read: [Organizational Change Management](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/people-group/organizational-change-management/)

### 24. Describe how you identified a valuable opportunity and persuaded a group to deliver it.

*Behavioral · [Leading engineering teams](../themes/engineering-leadership.md)*

Build the answer around the opportunity, not around how persuasive you were. Start with what you noticed and why it mattered: which signal in the data, the support tickets or the metrics, what size of effect you expected and on what basis. Then the important part. Everyone you needed already had a plan for the quarter, so say whose priorities you were pushing against, what objections came back, and how the proposal changed because of other people's input; a coalition holds together through co-authorship, not through persuasion. A written document with options, risks and open questions helps here, because people argue with a text rather than with rumours. Then give what was actually delivered and what effect it had, and mark the limits of your influence honestly: where other people decided, and what did not work. The mistake is a story where you convinced everyone at once, with no losses.

Read: [Design Docs at Google](https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/) · [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

### 25. Walk through the most difficult product launch you led.

*Behavioral · [Programmes and delivery](../themes/program-delivery.md)*

Pick a launch where the difficulty was in the dependencies, not the volume of work, and open with the frame: the goal, the constraints on date, quality and regulatory requirements, who was involved, and what sat on the critical path. Then give the interviewer what they want most, which is one decision: what you actually decided, what the alternatives were, what data you had, and how you got agreement from the people it affected. Unpack that one in detail and compress everything else. Say how you defined readiness, with release criteria, a rollback plan and on-call cover after the release; that is what separates managing risk from hoping. Finish with the outcome in the terms you promised beforehand, and what you changed for later launches. The usual mistake is a project overview with no contribution of your own; the second is a victory report where no bet went wrong.

Read: [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/) · [Design Docs at Google](https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/)

### 26. Three weeks before launching an LLM feature, evaluation reveals substantial hallucinations on edge cases. What happens next?

*Applied scenario · [Programmes and delivery](../themes/program-delivery.md)*

The first thing I do is stop discussing the date and establish the shape of the risk: how severe the consequences of this error are, how often it appears on the real distribution of requests, who it hits, and how trustworthy the evaluation itself is, since a small or unrepresentative eval set can both exaggerate a problem and hide it. I compare the options on one scale of harm and cost: narrow the feature to the cases where it's reliable, add human review or an honest refusal, fix the cause in retrieval and prompts, or move the launch. Each option pays something: narrowing costs value, a human in the loop costs speed and money. I name an owner for the launch decision, written exit criteria, and a communication plan for users and support. None of this helps if the edge-case error is irreversible: then there's no launch to discuss.

Read: [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) · [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

### 27. Describe a large cross-functional project, including ambiguity, roadblocks and delays.

*Behavioral · [Programmes and delivery](../themes/program-delivery.md)*

What's tested here isn't stamina, it's how you change the way you work as the picture clears. Start with the map: what you promised to deliver, what those deliverables depended on, and who personally owned each dependency, because people are accountable, not teams. Then take one blockage and show the mechanics: which signal let you see it rather than hear about it afterwards, what you changed in the plan, the order of work or the escalation path, and what you gave up to do it. Keep three things apart: what was delivered, what effect it had, and how that compares with the original target; if the target was missed, say so. The common mistake is a long coordination story with no decision in it. Finish with what you now do earlier, which is usually an early test of the most fragile dependency.

Read: [Design Docs at Google](https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/) · [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

### 28. How would you roll out updates to Alexa devices already deployed in people's homes?

*System design · [Programmes and delivery](../themes/program-delivery.md)*

Updating home devices means operating in someone else's environment: different models and firmware versions, weak Wi-Fi, a socket switched off halfway through the install. I assess: changes, affected devices, whether protocol compatibility with older versions holds, how large the package is and when to download it so the user isn't disturbed. Then I ship in waves: our own devices, a small group, then wider cohorts with a health check after install and a metric of devices that came back online, not just ones that received the package. The install has to be atomic, with a backup image and an automatic return to the previous version after a failed boot or health check. I set the thresholds for pausing the rollout, the owner of the rollback call, and what support will see. None of this saves you from a defect in the update mechanism itself: that may require a service visit.

Read: [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

### 29. A customer wants to automate claims processing with AI. What would you do in the first two weeks?

*Applied scenario · [Applied and customer scenarios](../themes/applied-scenarios.md)*

I'd use those two weeks to define one measurable process. First I take apart how claims are handled today: which steps exist, which decisions a person makes and by what rules, where exceptions come up, how frequent they are, and who actually works in the system every day. In parallel I check the data: whether we have access, what form the documents are in, what counts as a correct answer, and whether there is a decision history to give us a baseline. Separately I look at the cost of an error, because a wrongful denial and an overpayment cost different things, and that decides which steps stay with a human. By the end I pick a narrow pilot: one claim type, an end-to-end path, a baseline on time and accuracy, acceptance criteria, and an owner on the customer side. Automating the whole flow is not on the table yet.

Read: [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

### 30. A customer executive wants to cancel an AI pilot because it keeps producing wrong results. What would you do over the next 48 hours?

*Applied scenario · [Applied and customer scenarios](../themes/applied-scenarios.md)*

In the first hours I acknowledge the problem plainly, with no explanation of how it happened: trust is gone, and an argument about wording finishes it. I ask for specifics, not "it works badly" but a dozen real cases with the request, the answer they got, and the answer it should have been. That is the only way to separate three different illnesses: data that's missing or dirty, defects in the system itself such as retrieval and prompts, and expectations that never matched what the feature can do. I contain the damage: I switch off the riskiest scenarios and put human review or an honest refusal where confidence is low. By the end of the second day I propose a short recovery stage with a fixed set of cases, a deadline, and explicit continue-or-stop criteria. If the root cause is expectations, closing the pilot is more honest than fixing symptoms.

Read: [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/) · [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

### 31. A customer insists on fine-tuning their own model on support tickets, while you suspect retrieval would be enough. How do you proceed?

*Applied scenario · [Applied and customer scenarios](../themes/applied-scenarios.md)*

I don't start with an architecture argument. I start by asking what the customer is trying to solve with their own model: different behaviour and output format, knowledge that isn't in the context, a different cost per request, or control over the weights and where they run. Those four needs are met differently, and fine-tuning covers the first one well: it freezes knowledge at training time and ages along with the support tickets, while retrieval over their data updates when someone edits the source. Then I build a representative task set from their own tickets with expected answers, and compare the approaches on it honestly, hybrid included. Before recommending anything I talk through the cost of ownership: labelling, data quality, retraining when the base model changes, evaluation, migration. If the requirement comes from a regulator or from data isolation, arguing about quality is beside the point.

Read: [Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml) · [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

### 32. A deployed agent's base model will be retired in 60 days. How would you migrate it without losing quality?

*Applied scenario · [Applied and customer scenarios](../themes/applied-scenarios.md)*

I would treat sixty days as a deadline to assess, not a guarantee of enough time. First I inventory workflows, prompts, tool contracts and dependencies on model quirks: answer formats, context limits, refusals and accumulated workarounds. In parallel I freeze an evaluation set covering typical tasks and known failures, so successor selection rests on evidence. I compare candidates on quality, latency and cost, budgeting for prompt and parser changes. Migration proceeds through small traffic slices, during staffed hours, with advance customer communication. Before retirement, rollback may use the old model; afterward it needs a supported alternative or a reduced service mode. Tasks without objective correctness criteria require human review, whose lead time belongs in the plan. If migration cannot finish safely, I communicate scope reductions and contingency plans early.

Read: [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) · [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

### 33. A customer says their eight-GPU chatbot is too slow and too expensive. You have a week with them; how do you use it?

*Applied scenario · [Applied and customer scenarios](../themes/applied-scenarios.md)*

I'd start the week with measurements, not ideas: what the real workload profile looks like, how latency is distributed across percentiles rather than averaged, what the response time is made of, retrieval, prefill, decode, external calls, what the utilisation of those eight GPUs is, and what one successfully completed user task costs. The customer's complaint is usually about that last number, not about the price of a token. I profile first and only then pick the lever: batching and serving parameters, a smaller model or quantisation, shorter context and more precise retrieval, streaming and caching for perceived speed. That order holds because swapping the model is the most expensive move and serving is often underloaded. Every change gets validated on the same recorded workload with quality guardrails. If the bottleneck is in the data sources or in the scenario itself, optimising inference won't help.

Read: [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/) · [Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)

### 34. An enterprise wants document Q&A over two million internal files within four weeks, with no data leaving its VPC. How would you scope the pilot?

*Applied scenario · [Applied and customer scenarios](../themes/applied-scenarios.md)*

Four weeks and two million files is a conversation about choosing, not about coverage. First I narrow it down: which document collections are genuinely needed, who has rights to them today, which services are allowed inside the perimeter, and which fifteen or so employee questions are worth the most. Permissions are not post-processing: the index has to carry labels and retrieval has to filter by the asker's rights, or the pilot becomes a leak path of its own. Then I take a representative slice of the data rather than a random one: it needs current and stale documents, duplicates and mixed formats, because those are what break answer quality. I build the end-to-end path in full, even on a narrow slice. Up front I agree acceptance tests, an owner for operations, and what the pilot will not prove: load, full coverage, and cost at the full volume.

Read: [Architect multitenant solutions on Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/overview) · [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

### 35. A shopping agent can initiate payments. How would you prove that each payment matches the user's actual authorisation?

*System design · [Payments and regulated domains](../themes/domain-payments-fintech.md)*

A payment has to rest on a separate verifiable authorisation, not on what the agent understood the user to mean. Intent is expressed as an explicit object with constraints, amount or limit, payee, currency, validity period and conditions, and it's signed so it can be produced later; that's what AP2 is built on, where signed mandates tie the user's consent to a specific purchase and payment and give a consistent trail. Authority is validated at execution time on the payment side: if the amount or the payee falls outside the grant, you need a new confirmation, not the agent's guess. The audit trail keeps what the user approved, what the agent proposed and what executed. Authorisation evidence and settlement are different things: an authorisation doesn't mean the money arrived. A signature authenticates a signer and unchanged mandate; genuine consent also requires a trusted approval flow. Limits and revocation still matter.

Read: [AP2 - Agent Payments Protocol Documentation](https://ap2-protocol.org/)

### 36. An AI support agent initiates a refund, then the payment API times out. How should the system recover without issuing the refund twice?

*System design · [Payments and regulated domains](../themes/domain-payments-fintech.md)*

A timeout does not mean the refund failed, so I'd treat the unknown outcome as a reconciliation problem rather than a reason to repeat the call. Every operation gets a stable identifier created before the first request, and the intent is persisted in our own database before the request goes out, otherwise a retry has nothing to attach to. The retry goes with the same idempotency key under the provider's contract, with exponential backoff and jitter; if the response is ambiguous again, the status is resolved with a status query or by reconciling reports, not with a second refund. You have to account for the finite lifetime of keys, concurrent attempts under one key, and a changed amount, which makes it a different operation. I'd test parallel retries and the manual escalation path. There is no end to end exactly once: this is retry with deduplication and later reconciliation.

Read: [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

### 37. A bank wants to roll out an AI assistant that proposes case decisions to employees. What evidence and controls would you require before expansion?

*Applied scenario · [Payments and regulated domains](../themes/domain-payments-fintech.md)*

Before expanding you have to fix which decisions the assistant touches, which customers they affect, and where its authority ends: it proposes, the employee decides, and that has to be true in the interface, not just in a document. I would collect two kinds of evidence: a set of real cases with known correct outcomes, including rare and expensive errors, and the behaviour of employees, the share of suggestions accepted and rejected, and reversals and corrections after acceptance. The mechanism is uncomfortable: a suggestion shifts attention, and agreement quickly becomes a formality, so suggestion quality is measured together with the quality of human decisions. Then you name owners, monitoring, the escalation path and a staged expansion by segment with a stop ready, and the applicable jurisdiction requirements are verified separately with lawyers. Quality on historical cases does not predict behaviour with new products and unfamiliar fraud schemes.

Read: [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

### 38. Why do you want to work at Anthropic, and where do you disagree with its approach?

*Self-presentation · [Behavioral and values](../themes/behavioral-values.md)*

Build the motivation on verifiable specifics: name a paper, a product or a company decision you actually studied, and explain how it connects to your work and to what you want to do next. Generic mission statements tell the interviewer little about you. The second half of the question matters more than the first. The disagreement has to be real, with a clear basis, and it must come with an answer to what evidence or results would change your position; that is what separates judgement from a pose. Take the subject from the substance of the work, not a safe detail and not an accusation. Finish with how you would work while holding that disagreement: what you contribute, how you raise the objection internally, and why you carry out a decision that went against you. Refresh the facts from the company's public material before the conversation.

Read: [Careers](https://www.anthropic.com/careers)

### 39. Describe a mistake you made, its consequences and what you changed afterward.

*Behavioral · [Behavioral and values](../themes/behavioral-values.md)*

Pick a mistake that genuinely cost money, time or trust, or the answer turns into hidden boasting. Start with the decision: what you chose, what you knew at the time, and why it looked reasonable, so the interviewer sees your thinking and not just the outcome. Then the consequences and the recovery, without spreading the blame across circumstances and colleagues: a blameless postmortem means an honest analysis of causes, not a way of dropping your own responsibility. The most common failure in this answer is the line about taking on too much, which dresses a virtue up as a flaw. Finish with a change that stayed with you, a different rule for deciding, a check before release, the habit of writing the postmortem, and with a sign that it worked, for example a similar situation that went differently the next time.

Read: [Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/)

### 40. Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone and could not persuade them.

*Behavioral · [Behavioral and values](../themes/behavioral-values.md)*

What matters in this answer is what happened after the argument, not the argument itself. Put both positions fairly and in their strongest form: if the other side sounds stupid, the interviewer decides you were listening badly. Give your own evidence and how you put it across, in conversation, in a written document, through data. Then say clearly who made the decision and why it was theirs to make, and describe how you backed the agreed action: you object before the decision, and after it you deliver, without quiet sabotage. Name the result, even if it proved you right, but without any triumph. Mark the limit as well: what you would not have done, and in what situation you would escalate. Finish with the conclusion, usually about what your argument was missing or who you should have gone to earlier.

Read: [Leadership Principles](https://amazon.jobs/content/en/our-workplace/leadership-principles)
